\begin{abstract}
% BEGIN sections/abstract.tex
% Abstract. Numbers are generated macros (report/generated/numbers.tex).
An idle superconducting qubit waiting during a neighbour's mid-circuit measurement loses
coherence to stochastic dephasing and to deterministic frequency shifts. We ask whether
model-based optimization of dynamical-decoupling (DD) pulse timings and phases with CMA-ES
outperforms strong canonical sequences. To answer it fairly, we pre-registered a synthetic
transmon-like model, seeds, baselines and a training-only baseline-selection rule, and scored
every arm on independent held-out noise. A finite-pulse Monte-Carlo simulator agrees with
filter-function theory in five predetermined configurations (largest $|z|=\GthreeMaxZ$).
Synthetic Ramsey/Hahn/CPMG spectroscopy recovers a predictive noise model (held-out RMSE
$\SpecGaussFullRmseRatio\times$ the shot-noise floor), but the spectrum is not uniquely
identified. In the pre-registered Scenario~A, no CMA-ES mode delivered a practically meaningful gain over the selected XY4/XY8 baseline,
whose infidelity ($\BenchASixteenSelEps$ at $n=16$) is already at the $T_1$-plus-white-noise
floor ($\FloorA$). With a deterministic Stark-like shift and virtual-$Z$ correction, CMA-ES
beat XY4 by a few percent at the nominal profile only at $n=4$. The timing+phase variant of that
gain reversed under the pre-registered $\pm100$\,ns readout-timing shifts, and only phase-only
sequences kept a marginal, model-specific advantage. Optimizing on fitted models, or with more
headroom, did not help, and training gains did not generalize. All results are synthetic; no quantum hardware was used.

% END sections/abstract.tex
\end{abstract}
\begin{IEEEkeywords}
dynamical decoupling, superconducting qubits, noise spectroscopy,
CMA-ES, synthetic simulation, quantum control
\end{IEEEkeywords}
% BEGIN sections/introduction.tex
\section{Introduction and project bounds}
\label{sec:intro}
% ~0.75 page. Motivation (IQCC/Columbia), idle qubit during mid-circuit measurement (MCM),
% metrics, hypotheses and scope.

\paragraph{Motivation} The project originates from a course project-ideas brief
\citep{QMBrief2026}; that brief is not evidence that this implementation exists
or that hardware access has been provisioned. Prospective use of IQCC hardware remains
unconfirmed: no access, authorization or hardware run exists for this report.

\paragraph{Problem} An idle qubit accumulates phase errors from stochastic dephasing and, in
dynamic circuits, from deterministic frequency shifts during neighbouring readout. We ask
whether model-based optimization of DD sequences can reduce idle-window infidelity relative to
strong canonical baselines under a fixed pulse budget and identical constraints.

\paragraph{Research questions}
\begin{description}
  \item[RQ1] Agreement of Monte Carlo coherence with analytic filter-function predictions under
    matched PSD conventions.
  \item[RQ2] Predictive (held-out) accuracy of noise parameters fitted from synthetic
    Ramsey, Hahn and CPMG data.
  \item[RQ3] Whether joint optimization of pulse timings and phases beats strong DD baselines in
    Scenario~A (stochastic dephasing) on held-out noise.
  \item[RQ4] Whether any gain over calibrated virtual-$Z$ and standard DD survives uncertainty
    in readout-induced detuning (Scenario~B).
  \item[RQ5] Robustness to pulse imperfections, drift, calibration error, PSD misspecification and
    control quantization.
\end{description}

\paragraph{Scope} Synthetic simulations only. Scenarios, seeds, baselines, the
baseline-selection rule and the metrics were pre-registered in the repository before any
optimization run; deviations are logged. A zero gain or a regression counts as a valid outcome. Metric: average gate infidelity against the corrected target
(Sec.~\ref{sec:model}).

% END sections/introduction.tex
% BEGIN sections/related_work.tex
\section{Related work}
\label{sec:related}
% ~0.75 page. Each sentence maps to a LIT-xx claim in report/claims.json.
% Primary arXiv identities were checked in a later audit; consult docs/CITATION_AUDIT.md.

% LIT-01
Dynamical decoupling of open quantum systems was introduced by \citet{Viola1999}.
% LIT-02
\citet{Uhrig2007} proposed optimized $\pi$-pulse sequences for keeping a qubit coherent,
% LIT-03
and \citet{Cywinski2008} analysed how to enhance dephasing times in superconducting qubits.
% LIT-04
\citet{Biercuk2009} studied optimized DD in a model quantum memory.
% LIT-05, LIT-06
DD has also been used for noise spectroscopy: \citet{Bylander2011} with a superconducting flux
qubit and \citet{Alvarez2011} for colored noise.
% LIT-07
Robust DD was studied by \citet{Souza2011},
% LIT-08
and \citet{Ezzell2023} surveyed DD performance on superconducting qubits.
% LIT-09, LIT-10, LIT-11
Learning-based approaches to choosing DD sequences include \citet{Rahman2024}, \citet{Tong2025}
and \citet{Tong2026}.

\paragraph{Empirical versus model-based}
% LIT-10 (title only)
Of the learning-based works, only the title of \citet{Tong2025} states the setting: its learning
is described as empirical and carried out on quantum processors, i.e.\ hardware in the loop.
% LIT-09, LIT-11
The published abstract of \citet{Tong2026} describes empirical optimization of
DD in dynamic quantum circuits, including measurement and feedforward; the present work,
by contrast, is synthetic and model-based. Publisher-version metadata and citation details remain separately tracked (\repopath{docs/CITATION\_AUDIT.md}).

\paragraph{Positioning}
% No LIT claim: describes this project only. Novelty claim deliberately limited.
This project is a model-based, synthetic-only study: sequences are optimized and evaluated
against a simulated noise model, and no quantum hardware has been used.
Its contribution is limited to a pre-registered, held-out synthetic benchmark of model-based DD
optimization with explicit noise floors.
Its main finding is negative: under the pre-registered synthetic model, CMA-ES did not
provide a practically meaningful generalizable improvement over XY4/XY8 on held-out noise (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}).
A synthetic benchmark of this kind does not test whether its conclusions transfer to hardware.

% END sections/related_work.tex
% BEGIN sections/model.tex
\section{Physical model and conventions}
\label{sec:model}
% ~0.75 page. Conventions follow docs/PHYSICS_CONVENTIONS.md (integration-lead owned).
% Definitions only. Derivations: docs/PHYSICS.md.

We use $\hbar=1$, time in s, angular frequency and detuning in rad/s and angles in rad. In the
rotating frame of the drive,
\begin{multline}
  H(t) = \tfrac{1}{2}\bigl[\delta(t) + d(t) + \delta_{\mathrm{off}}\bigr]\sigma_z\\
       + \tfrac{1}{2}\Omega(t)\bigl[\cos\varphi(t)\,\sigma_x + \sin\varphi(t)\,\sigma_y\bigr],
\end{multline}
where $\delta(t)$ is zero-mean stationary noise, assumed \emph{Gaussian} unless stated
otherwise, $d(t)$ a known deterministic detuning profile (e.g.\ during neighbouring readout),
and $\delta_{\mathrm{off}}$ a static calibration offset.

\paragraph{Spectrum and filter} With autocorrelation
$C(\tau)=\langle\delta(t+\tau)\delta(t)\rangle$ we use the \emph{two-sided} PSD
$S_2(\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} C(\tau)e^{-i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$ in rad$^2$/s.
For the switching function $y(t)$ (toggling-frame $z$ component, $\pm1$ between ideal $\pi$
pulses),
\begin{gather}
  Y(\omega)=\int_0^T y(t)e^{i\omega t}\,dt,\\
  \chi=\operatorname{Var}\phi=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} S_2(\omega)\,|Y(\omega)|^2\,d\omega,
\end{gather}
and, under the Gaussian assumption, $W=e^{-\chi/2}$ with pure-dephasing average gate infidelity
$r=(1-W)/3$. Low- and high-frequency cutoffs of $S_2$ are stated explicitly for every model.

\paragraph{Energy relaxation} $T_1$ is modelled as amplitude damping with
$\gamma=1-e^{-t/T_1}$ per free segment; channels are composed as Pauli transfer matrices, never
by adding infidelities. Amplitude damping alone has average infidelity
$r_{\rm AD}=(2+\gamma-2\sqrt{1-\gamma})/6\approx\gamma/3$ (derived in \repopath{docs/PHYSICS.md} and
checked numerically against Haar and six-state averages).

\paragraph{Target and frame correction} Fidelity is evaluated against
$U_{\mathrm{target}}=R_z(\theta_{\mathrm{vz}})U_0$, where $U_0$ is the ideal net control
unitary of the sequence and $\theta_{\mathrm{vz}}$ is a virtual-$Z$ correction of the known
$d(t)$ (zero unless frame correction is allowed). Average gate fidelity of a channel with PTM
$R$ is $F_{\mathrm{avg}}=(\operatorname{Tr}R+2)/6$ evaluated on $R_{\mathrm{target}}^{\mathsf T}R$.
For finite pulses we use the generalized (three-component toggling-frame) filter function, so
$W=e^{-\chi/2}$ is exact only for instantaneous pulses and leading-order otherwise; the
Monte-Carlo simulator needs neither approximation.
Finite pulse widths, minimum spacing and timing-grid constraints are enforced for all sequences.

% END sections/model.tex
% BEGIN sections/methods.tex
\section{Methods}
\label{sec:methods}
% Describes only what the code implements (src/ddopt/*). All numbers below come from
% configs/scenario_a.json (synthetic assumptions) or generated macros.

\paragraph{Synthetic device (Scenario~A)} All device numbers are \emph{synthetic assumptions},
fixed in a pre-registered plan (\repopath{docs/EXPERIMENT\_PLAN.md}) before any optimization run.
The idle window is $T=2\,\mu$s (alternate $4\,\mu$s), with square $\pi$ pulses of width
$w=32$\,ns, a 4\,ns guard and pulse starts on a 4\,ns grid (an assumed controller tick).
The dephasing PSD is the sum of a band-limited $1/f$ term ($2\pi\cdot1$\,Hz--$2\pi\cdot10$\,MHz,
scaled so that the analytic Ramsey coherence is $e^{-1}$ at $10\,\mu$s), a Gaussian
Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (Lorentzian) term with $\tau_c=0.5\,\mu$s, and a white floor
$S_0=10^4$\,rad$^2$/s; $T_1=100\,\mu$s; and each trajectory draws a relative Rabi-amplitude error
$\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,0.02^2)$. Scenario~B adds a deterministic Stark-like shift of
$2\pi\cdot0.2$\,MHz between 0.6 and 1.6\,$\mu$s (20\,ns tanh edges) as a stand-in for a
neighbouring readout; it models a known frequency shift only, not measurement-induced
dephasing.

\paragraph{Finite-pulse Monte-Carlo simulator} Gaussian noise trajectories are sampled on a
1\,ns grid by spectral synthesis (exact Ornstein--Uhlenbeck recursion for the Lorentzian; exact
Markov jumps for telegraph noise). Free segments are exact $z$ rotations by the integrated
detuning; pulses are propagated in 8 piecewise-constant sub-steps, including detuning during the
pulse. Amplitude damping is composed per free segment (exact, as it is phase-covariant) and
approximated as $\mathrm{AD}(w/2)\,U\,\mathrm{AD}(w/2)$ during pulses. The noise-averaged Pauli
transfer matrix gives $F_{\rm avg}$ against the corrected target. The reported $\epsilon$ is the
mean of per-trajectory infidelities, which equals the channel infidelity because $F_{\rm avg}$ is
linear in the channel. Unit tests check unitarity ($<10^{-14}$), zero-noise compensated infidelity
($\le10^{-10}$ for all families, odd and even $n$), $O(\Delta t^2)$ and $O(m^{-2})$ convergence
in noise step and pulse sub-steps, and the $T_1$-only formula to $10^{-12}$.

\paragraph{Spectroscopy and held-out fits} Synthetic Ramsey, Hahn, CPMG-2 and CPMG-4 data
(14 log-spaced idle times in $[0.1,40]\,\mu$s, 1000 shots per point, binomial shot noise, an
affine SPAM map) are fitted by binomial maximum likelihood with a parametric bootstrap.
Two Gaussian models are fitted: \emph{reduced} ($1/f$ with $\alpha=1$, plus white) and
\emph{full} (reduced plus Lorentzian). $T_1$ is treated as known from a separate experiment,
because white dephasing and $1/T_1$ are degenerate for instantaneous pulses. Held-out data are
CPMG-8 and CPMG-16 at all times, and the training families at 13 unseen times, drawn with an
independent generator. The fit never sees held-out observations; a unit test asserts identical
parameters with and without test data. A misspecification control replaces the Lorentzian
with telegraph noise of equal second-order statistics.

\paragraph{CMA-ES optimization} We use pycma 4.5.0 \citep{Hansen2016}, an evolution
strategy rather than reinforcement learning. Timings are encoded by $n$ unconstrained
coordinates, giving gaps $g_k=g_{\min}+(T-nw-(n+1)g_{\min})\,\mathrm{softmax}([0,z])_k$ with no
redundant shift; starts are snapped to the grid, and candidates that cannot be repaired are
rejected. Pulse phases are offsets from the base phases, projected so that the ideal net unitary
stays equal to the base sequence's ($\propto I$ or a Pauli). Fidelity is therefore never graded
against the wrong target. Three modes are run: timing-only and phase-only (both starting from
CPMG with $Y$ pulses) and timing+phase. Each run has a budget of 2000 objective evaluations on
256 frozen training trajectories (common random numbers). There are three independent training
runs (training seeds 101--103 with optimizer seeds 1--3).

\paragraph{Baselines, selection rule and evaluation} At each $n$, the baselines are CPMG-$n$
($Y$ pulses), XY4, XY8 (where $n$ divides), UDD-$n$ and free evolution, with the same $T$, $w$,
guard, grid, noise model and frame-correction privileges. The \emph{training-selected canonical} baseline is fixed
by a pre-registered rule: the lowest \emph{training} infidelity. All arms are then evaluated on
the same held-out test draws (seeds 9001--9005, 1024 trajectories each; disjointness from
training is enforced in code). We report raw $\epsilon$, the ratio
$\epsilon_{\rm selected}/\epsilon_{\rm CMA}$ (values $>1$ favour CMA-ES), and a two-stage paired
bootstrap 95\% interval (seeds as blocks, trajectories within seeds). These intervals quantify
Monte-Carlo uncertainty within the synthetic model only; they are not significance tests and do
not account for model selection or model mismatch.

\paragraph{Reproducibility} Each run writes an immutable \repopath{results/<run\_id>/} directory
with a manifest (UTC time, git SHA and dirty flag, platform, Python and package versions, config
hash, seeds, command) and SHA-256 checksums. Every table, figure and number macro in this report
is regenerated by \repopath{scripts/make\_report\_artifacts.py} from checksum-verified runs pinned
in \repopath{report/runs.json}; the claim ledger is \repopath{report/evidence\_map.csv}.
The historical full-suite record reports \GenTestSummary. Current CI executes the specified smoke suite independently.

% END sections/methods.tex
% BEGIN sections/results.tex
\section{Experimental Results}
\label{sec:results}
All results in this section are computed on \emph{synthetic} device models; no IQCC
hardware run has been performed. The experiment configurations, raw outputs, seeds,
reproduction commands, checksums and claim ledger are in the public repository
(\repopath{results/}, \repopath{report/evidence\_map.csv}). Extended tables,
ablation plots and individual trial analyses are included in the supplementary
report (\repopath{report/sections/results\_full.tex}).

\subsection{Simulator and Spectroscopy Validation}
In five predetermined configurations, Monte Carlo infidelity agrees with the
ideal filter-function reference within the specified combined uncertainty
(largest standardized discrepancy $|z|=\GthreeMaxZ$); this establishes internal
consistency, \emph{not} device validation. The Gaussian fit predicts 106
held-out synthetic decay measurements (Fig.~\ref{fig:spec}) with RMSE
$\SpecGaussFullRmseRatio\times$ the shot-noise floor and 95\% interval coverage
$\SpecGaussFullCov$. These predictions rely on the same analytic forward
family used to generate the data, fixed $T_1$ and known cutoffs.
The spectral model is not uniquely identified.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_spectroscopy.pdf}
\caption{Synthetic noise spectroscopy. (a) True and fitted two-sided PSD
with a 95\% bootstrap band; spectral uncertainty is substantial outside the
sampled passbands. (b) Fitted decay curves; open circles are independent
held-out points only.}
\label{fig:spec}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Scenario A: Canonical DD Versus Optimization}
With equal pulse count and independent held-out noise (Fig.~\ref{fig:bench}), no CMA-ES mode provides
a practically meaningful improvement over the training-selected XY4/XY8
baseline. In particular, the $n=16$ baseline infidelity
$\BenchASixteenSelEps$ is close to the simulated $T_1$-plus-white-noise
floor $\FloorA$. The largest held-out ratio $\epsilon_{\rm sel}/\epsilon_{\rm CMA}$ is
$\BenchAFourBothRatioHi$ (one $n=4$ timing+phase run): gains are at most about 1\%, which
is not practically meaningful and does not establish optimization headroom. Joint timing/phase optimization fits frozen
training trajectories more closely while degrading on independent evaluation,
consistent with overfitting under the tested budget and model.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_benchmark_ratio.pdf}
\caption{Held-out ratio $\epsilon_{\rm sel}/\epsilon_{\rm CMA}$ ($>1$ favours
CMA-ES) for each of three CMA-ES training runs, at the same $n$ and $T=2\,\mu$s
as the training-selected baseline named under each $n$. Bars: paired-bootstrap
95\% intervals (Monte-Carlo uncertainty within the model only). Timing-only
CMA-ES (ratios $\BenchASixteenTimingRatioLo$--$\BenchBFourTimingRatioHi$) is
omitted for clarity; raw infidelities are tabulated in the supplement.}
\label{fig:bench}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Scenario B: Readout-Like Detuning}
A deterministic, synthetic Stark-like frequency profile was added to the
idle window. The experiment does not model stochastic measurement-induced
dephasing or measured readout. The joint timing/phase optimization offers a
few-percent nominal advantage over XY4 plus virtual-$Z$ at $n=4$, but this
reverses for prescribed $\pm100$\,ns timing shifts. The phase-only $n=4$
candidate retains a small advantage in the tested perturbation sweep.
These positive cells were selected after examining multiple comparisons;
they are exploratory and cannot support a general hardware claim.

\subsection{Ablations and Interpretation}
Removing the white-noise and relaxation limits creates additional theoretical
headroom, but under the specified search budget CMA-ES gained less than 0.5\% over
XY8 at $n=8$ in held-out evaluation (ratios up to $\AblColoredEightPhaseRatioHi$,
colored-only phase-only, and $\AblNoToneEightBothRatioHi$, no-$T_1$ timing+phase) and
lost substantially at $n=16$ (colored-only timing+phase, ratio
$\AblColoredSixteenBothRatioLo$--$\AblColoredSixteenBothRatioHi$). The fitted-model pipeline further exposes simulation
to model mismatch. Overall, canonical robust DD is a difficult baseline
to beat in the tested regimes; the synthetic results do not rule out
advantages from alternative noise spectra, optimizers, or real hardware.

% END sections/results.tex
% BEGIN sections/discussion.tex
\section{Discussion, limitations and roadmap}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Interpretation} Under the pre-registered model the answer to RQ3 is negative. XY4/XY8
already suppress the decouplable colored noise, and the remaining infidelity is set by $T_1$
and white dephasing, which ideal refocusing pulses do not suppress in this model. Where headroom exists (the
colored-only ablation), our CMA-ES setup gained under 0.5\% over XY8 at $n=8$ on held-out noise
and lost substantially at $n=16$. Its training
improvements came from fitting the finite set of frozen trajectories, and the timing+phase
search starting from CPMG did not reach XY8's robustness to amplitude errors within 2000
evaluations. These are statements about this parameterization, budget and synthetic model, not
about CMA-ES or learned DD in general. The one positive signal (Scenario~B, $n=4$) is a few
percent and was identified after the fact. Its timing+phase form does not survive
readout-timing uncertainty; its phase-only form does, but only within this model. It would need
a new pre-registered test before any claim.

\needspace{5\baselineskip}
\paragraph{Limitations}
\begin{itemize}
  \item All evidence is synthetic. Device parameters are assumptions, not measurements, and
    optimizing against a model one also evaluates on is circular; the fitted-model pipeline
    shows that identification error only adds loss.
  \item Noise is Gaussian and stationary (except in the telegraph control, which is near-Gaussian
    at our parameters). Non-stationary, measurement-induced dephasing during readout is
    \emph{not} modelled; Scenario~B is a known deterministic frequency shift only.
  \item $T_1$ during pulses is approximated; leakage, crosstalk, finite bandwidth and pulse
    shaping are absent. Pulse errors are a static per-trajectory amplitude error.
  \item Monte-Carlo intervals capture sampling uncertainty within the model only; with 5 test
    seeds the seed-level variability is coarsely resolved. The colored-only, no-$T_1$,
    no-amplitude-error and convergence analyses were added after seeing the pre-registered
    results and are exploratory. One plumbing smoke run touched the test seeds before the main
    run (documented in \repopath{docs/EXPERIMENT\_PLAN.md}).
  \item Robustness of the optimized sequences to calibration drift, Stark rise time and
    timing-grid quantization (plan item P5.2) was not evaluated. The exploratory ablations reused
    the held-out test seeds, and the spectroscopy and benchmark bootstraps share one seed.
  \item Earlier runs recorded the git state at manifest write time rather than run
    start, and $\PinnedRunsDirty$ of the $\PinnedRunsTotal$ pinned runs record a dirty
    working tree without the uncommitted diff: the \PinnedRunsDirtyList. These include
    pre-registered runs and the source of the spectroscopy headline numbers. Their SHA-256
    checksums prove that the stored files are unchanged, not which code produced them.
    Runs now record the start-of-run git state and diff, which cannot recover the earlier
    uncommitted code (\repopath{docs/REVIEW\_FINDINGS.md}).
  \item The original citation audit environment blocked primary sources; a later
    audit checked public arXiv reference identities. Publication metadata and
    final bibliographic presentation are documented in \repopath{docs/CITATION\_AUDIT.md}.
  \item No quantum-hardware execution was performed. The QUA adapter is an
    SDK-free schedule translator marked \emph{not hardware tested}; the QM SDK serialization
    test was skipped because the SDK is not installed in the project environment.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{Independent review} An AI red-team pass (\repopath{docs/REVIEW\_FINDINGS.md})
independently re-derived the conventions, reproduced several reported numbers bit-for-bit and
found no critical defect. Its high-severity finding (the Scenario~B timing+phase gain is not
robust) is incorporated above. Human review of the evidence ledger is pending.

\paragraph{Roadmap} (i) Measure, with authorization, $T_1$, Ramsey, Hahn and CPMG decays and
spectator phase during neighbour readout on the target device
(\repopath{docs/HARDWARE\_PROTOCOL.md}), to see whether the decouplable colored component is
large enough for optimization to matter at all. (ii) Model measurement-induced dephasing as
non-stationary noise and repeat Scenario~B. (iii) Regularize the optimizer (more training
trajectories, robust objectives, starting from XY8) and pre-register a new held-out benchmark.

\section{Detailed Synthetic Experiments and Results}
\label{supp:sec:results}
% Every number below is a macro from report/generated/numbers.tex (scripts/make_report_artifacts.py),
% traced in report/evidence_map.csv to a results/<run_id>/ artifact. All results are SYNTHETIC.

All results are \emph{simulation predictions for the synthetic model} of
Sec.~\ref{sec:methods}; none is a measurement. Each table and figure names the recorded
run it comes from; the full claim-to-artifact ledger is \repopath{report/evidence\_map.csv}.

\paragraph{RQ1: Monte Carlo versus filter function (gate G3)}
Table~\ref{supp:tab:g3} lists five predetermined configurations: free evolution, Hahn and CPMG-8, the
last two with both 32\,ns and instantaneous pulses. In every configuration the finite-pulse
Monte-Carlo infidelity agrees with the analytic prediction within $1.96$ standard errors
($\GthreeNtraj$ trajectories per case; largest $|z|=\GthreeMaxZ$). Halving the noise step changes
each estimate by less than the combined statistical error of the two runs. The PSD normalization, filter function,
noise sampler and propagator are therefore mutually consistent at the resolution of this test
(standard errors of $\GthreeRelSELo$--$\GthreeRelSEHi\%$ of $r$). This is a consistency check between two implementations of the same model, not
evidence about any device.

\paragraph{RQ2: spectroscopy and held-out prediction (gate G4)}
Figure~\ref{supp:fig:spec} and Table~\ref{supp:tab:spectroscopy} summarize the pre-registered spectroscopy
run. With the correctly specified full Gaussian model, every fitted parameter's 95\% bootstrap
interval contains the truth. On 106 held-out points (new pulse counts and unseen idle times) the
RMSE is $\SpecGaussFullRmseRatio\times$ the shot-noise floor and the 95\% predictive coverage is
$\SpecGaussFullCov$. The reduced model (no Lorentzian) predicts worse
($\SpecGaussRedRmseRatio\times$ floor, coverage $\SpecGaussRedCov$), but our pre-set failure
thresholds do not flag it. For this seed the bootstrap intervals for $T_2^\ast$ and
$T_2^{\rm Hahn}$ narrowly exclude the true values ($\SpecTruthTtwoStar$ and
$\SpecTruthTtwoHahn\,\mu$s), even though each parameter interval covers. With a single recorded
seed we cannot tell whether this is chance or a systematic bias of the derived-time intervals;
a multi-seed coverage study is future work. This is a favourable test: the data are
generated by the same analytic (instantaneous-pulse, Gaussian) forward model that is fitted,
$T_1$ and the $1/f$ cutoffs are fixed at their true values, and only one data seed is
recorded. Some parameter intervals are wide (e.g.\ the white-noise level spans four orders of
magnitude), so only the derived decay predictions, not the individual spectral parameters,
are well constrained.

The spectrum is \emph{not} uniquely reconstructed. The Lorentzian $(\sigma,\tau_c)$ is strongly
correlated and weakly identified; the band above $\sim\!1$\,MHz spans orders of magnitude
(Fig.~\ref{supp:fig:spec}a); white dephasing and $1/T_1$ are degenerate; and the $1/f$ low cutoff
is not identifiable. The telegraph misspecification control is nearly Gaussian at Scenario~A
parameters (motional narrowing), so it does not stress the Gaussian assumption; the full model
fits it well (RMSE $\SpecTelFullRmseRatio\times$ floor). This control is therefore weak.

\paragraph{RQ3: CMA-ES versus canonical DD, Scenario~A (pre-registered)}
Table~\ref{supp:tab:bench} and Figs.~\ref{supp:fig:bench} and~\ref{supp:fig:benchratio} report held-out infidelities. The training-only
rule selects XY4 at $n=4$ and XY8 at $n=8,16$, with
$\epsilon=\BenchAFourSelEps$, $\BenchAEightSelEps$ and $\BenchASixteenSelEps$. No CMA-ES mode
gives a practically relevant improvement: the best single run (timing+phase, $n=4$) has ratio
$\BenchAFourBothRatioHi$ with an interval that includes 1, and the other modes are within
$\pm0.2\%$ or worse:
\begin{itemize}
  \item \textbf{Phase-only:} ratios $\BenchASixteenPhaseRatioLo$--$\BenchAFourPhaseRatioHi$
    (\(\approx1\)). The phases it finds are not XY-type: at $n=4$ they form a sign-alternated
    single-axis pattern ($a,\bar a,\bar a,a$), and at $n=8,16$ they are non-canonical. Several
    different phase patterns therefore reach the same floor.
  \item \textbf{Timing+phase:} ratios $\BenchAFourBothRatioLo$--$\BenchAFourBothRatioHi$ at $n=4$
    and at most $\BenchASixteenBothRatioHi$ at $n=8,16$.
  \item \textbf{Timing-only:} ratios as low as $\BenchASixteenTimingRatioLo$. This mode keeps
    CPMG's $Y$ axes, and CPMG with a 2\% amplitude error is far worse than XY4/XY8 under
    gate-fidelity grading (Table~\ref{supp:tab:bench}).
\end{itemize}
The reason there is nothing to gain is physical. XY8 reaches $\BenchASixteenSelEps$, essentially
the pulse-independent floor of $\FloorA$ set by $T_1$ and the white dephasing component
(dashed line in Fig.~\ref{supp:fig:bench}). Under the pre-registered model, no DD sequence can do
much better than XY8. At $T=4\,\mu$s, timing+phase is worse than XY8 (ratio
$\BenchATfourSixteenBothRatioLo$--$\BenchATfourSixteenBothRatioHi$ at $n=16$;
Table~\ref{supp:tab:ablation}).

\paragraph{Overfitting diagnostic} For a single training run at $n=8$ (exploratory; validation
seeds 8001--8002 are disjoint from the test seeds), the training infidelity of timing+phase
CMA-ES falls to $\ConvTrainFinal$, below XY8's training value. The validation infidelity stays at
$\ConvValFinal$, against $\ConvBestBaselineVal$ for XY8 (Fig.~\ref{supp:fig:conv}). The apparent
training gain comes from fitting the 256 frozen noise trajectories and does not generalize.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{figures/fig_convergence.pdf}
\caption{Training (dashed) versus validation (solid) infidelity of the best-so-far CMA-ES
candidate as a function of evaluation budget; Scenario~A, $n=8$, training seed 101.
Timing+phase starts from CPMG; timing-only keeps XY phases. The
horizontal lines show XY8. Exploratory diagnostic.}
\label{supp:fig:conv}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{RQ4: Scenario~B (deterministic Stark-like shift)}
At $n=8$, the four pre-registered arms reach $\epsilon=\BArmNoDD$ (no DD, no frame correction),
$\BArmVzOnly$ (virtual-$Z$ only), $\BArmDDVz$ (best canonical DD + virtual-$Z$) and
$\BArmCMAVz$ (CMA-ES + virtual-$Z$). Most of the benefit comes from frame correction plus any
XY-type DD. At the \emph{nominal} Stark profile, CMA-ES beats XY4+virtual-$Z$ only at $n=4$:
phase-only by ratios $\BenchBFourPhaseRatioLo$--$\BenchBFourPhaseRatioHi$ and timing+phase by
$\BenchBFourBothRatioLo$--$\BenchBFourBothRatioHi$ across the three training runs. The bracket
formed by the three per-run 95\% MC intervals is $\BenchBFourBothCILo$--$\BenchBFourBothCIHi$
for timing+phase. At $n=8,16$ there is no gain (Table~\ref{supp:tab:bench}). These $n=4$ cases were
picked out after inspecting about 27 Scenario~B comparisons, so they are exploratory.

The pre-registered robustness sweep (Table~\ref{supp:tab:robustness}, Fig.~\ref{supp:fig:rob}) changes
the picture for timing+phase. Under $\pm50$--$100$\,ns readout-timing shifts, its worst case
reaches $\RobBFourBothWorstMax$, against $\RobBFourDDWorst$ for XY4+virtual-$Z$, and it wins in
only $\RobBFourBothWinsMin$--$\RobBFourBothWinsMax$ of the 10 perturbed profiles. At $n=8$, two
of three runs lose in all 10. This nominal gain therefore does \emph{not} survive the
uncertainty RQ4 asks about. Only the $n=4$ phase-only sequences remain marginally better than
XY4+virtual-$Z$ in all 10 perturbations in all three runs (worst case
$\RobBFourPhaseWorstMax$ versus $\RobBFourDDWorst$), a few-percent, model-specific effect.
Virtual-$Z$ alone degrades to $\RobBFourVzWorst$ under a $\pm20\%$ amplitude error. Timing
shifts leave it unaffected, because the integrated phase of a shift that stays inside the window
is unchanged.

\paragraph{RQ5: robustness, ablations and model mismatch}
Table~\ref{supp:tab:ablation} adds post-hoc ablations, labelled exploratory. Removing $T_1$ and the
white floor (``colored only'') opens two orders of magnitude of headroom, since XY8 then reaches
$\AblColoredSixteenSelEps$ at $n=16$. Even so, timing+phase CMA-ES under the same 2000-evaluation
budget loses to XY8 (ratio $\AblColoredSixteenBothRatioLo$--$\AblColoredSixteenBothRatioHi$),
and phase-only gains at most $\AblColoredFourPhaseRatioHi$ at $n=4$. Within this budget and
parameterization (starting from CPMG, with $2n$ free coordinates), CMA-ES did not find sequences
that generalize better than XY-family designs. The training-only selection rule can itself pick
a baseline that is slightly worse on test (UDD in the no-amplitude-error ablation), which
inflates ratios there by $<1\%$. Robustness to calibration drift, Stark rise time and
timing-grid quantization of the optimized sequences (master-plan item P5.2) was \emph{not} run.
In the model-based pipeline
(Table~\ref{supp:tab:model_based}), optimizing on the noise model \emph{fitted} from synthetic
spectroscopy and testing on the truth gives ratios $\MBFitFullFourRatioLo$--$\MBFitFullFourRatioHi$
(full model, $n=4$) and $\MBFitRedFourRatioLo$--$\MBFitRedFourRatioHi$ (reduced model): model
error adds further loss, and with the reduced model the baseline-selection rule sometimes picks
the weaker family.
